entries.core_move: State the convolution theorem as the operational equivalence between continuous-time convolution and Fourier-domain multiplication, connecting direct LTI output convolution to frequency-domain signal analysis.
Convert $y(t)=x(t)*h(t) into Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega) to represent a convolution-based LTI system output in the Fourier domain$.
Compute the pointwise product $X(j\omega)$$H(j\omega)$ and interpret its magnitude and phase as the Fourier-domain representation of the time-domain convolution $x(t)$*$h(t)$.
Compare $y(t)=x(t)*h(t) with Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega) by deciding which domain gives the clearer computation or interpretation of an LTI system output$.

entries.lesson_title: Proof Idea of the Convolution Theorem
entries.core_move: Trace the proof idea of the convolution theorem by substituting the convolution integral into the Fourier transform definition, interchanging integration order, and recognizing the two individual spectra.

entries.lesson_title: Using the Convolution Theorem to Avoid Direct Convolution
entries.core_move: Convert a continuous-time LTI convolution problem into Fourier-domain multiplication by finding $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$, simplifying $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$, and inverse-transforming to recover $y(t)$.
